## Introduction


- Liver transplantation (LT) has evolved from a high-risk procedure to a standard treatment for liver failure
- Successful liver replacement: 1-year survival >85%, 5-year survival >70%
- Despite dramatic outcome improvements, a significant percentage of patients experience life-threatening complications requiring reoperation

## Changing Demographics of Transplant Recipients

- Historically, hepatitis C cirrhosis was the main indication for LT in Europe and North America
- With effective antiviral therapy, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is quickly becoming the most common indication
- Rapid increase in NASH resulting in decompensated liver failure
- Anticipated increase in end-stage liver disease (ESLD)-related deaths by 178% by 2030

## The Obesity Epidemic and LT Complications

The obesity epidemic has had a 2-fold effect on LT complications:

1. Increasing the demand for livers
2. Increasing the prevalence of fatty liver disease in potential organ donors

- Fatty liver disease → increased number of discarded livers from brain-dead donors
- Increased number of transplanted liver grafts with higher macrosteatosis
- BMI >30 associated with increased postoperative cardiopulmonary complications and longer ICU stays

## Impact of Macrosteatosis on Outcomes

- Survival rates with macrosteatosis >30% are comparable to donors with less fatty liver disease
- However, postoperative complication rates are markedly increased:
  - Postreperfusion syndrome (PRS)
  - Early allograft dysfunction (EAD)
  - Postoperative dialysis
  - Need for a second operation

## Expanding the Donor Pool

Surgical techniques to increase the donor pool:

- Reduced-size grafts
- Split-liver grafts

With liver parenchymal-splitting operations came a new series of complications unique to these procedures:

- Hepatic artery thrombosis (HAT)
- Bile leaks
- Strictures

These are at least **two times higher** in living-donor graft recipients versus cadaveric graft recipients

## Small-for-Size Syndrome (SFSS)

- A major complication after LDLT
- Characterized by:
  - Hyperbilirubinemia
  - Coagulopathy
  - Encephalopathy
- Observed shortly after transplant
- Terminology becoming historic — EAD is now a more appropriate term
- Graft size is not the only factor for slow return of hepatic function

## Living Donor vs Deceased Donor Outcomes

- Despite higher morbidity in living-donor graft recipients, patient and graft survival are similar or superior to deceased donors
- There is a learning curve for reducing complications
- Chapter reviews common early and late complications encountered during and after LT
- Because complications after LT represent a continuum, most can occur at any time after surgery

## Procurement Injury to the Graft

- The process begins with identification of a suitable organ for a particular recipient
- Procurement teams are dispatched for recovery of various organs
- The liver procurement team dictates conduct of dissection below the diaphragm
- Cardiac team works in concert with the thoracic team if lungs and heart are also recovered

## Coordination of Multiorgan Procurement

- Infradiaphragmatic dissection takes considerably longer than thoracic dissection
- Careful planning required to minimize cold-ischemia time for heart and lungs (more time sensitive)
- Heart procurement team stays in contact with recipient heart team to minimize total ischemic time
- Under ideal conditions, the operation is orderly and well controlled

## Challenges in Unstable Brain-Dead Donors

- A patient who progresses to brain death rapidly can show cardiac instability
- Can be difficult to manage → expedited operation
- Perfusion cannulae hastily placed; organ procurement rapidly follows
- Identification of appropriate anatomy is difficult
- Technical errors are more likely to occur

## Donation After Cardiac Death (DCD)

- Gained popularity since the 1990s to increase available organs
- Estimated DCD organs could increase donor pool by 10% in 2010
- UNOS data: DCD donors increased from 6% to 11% of all US donors (2010–2019)
- Patient deemed hopeless but not meeting "brain death" criteria is allowed to die naturally after removal of supportive measures
- After 2 to 5 minutes of asystole (hospital policy dependent), organs can be procured

## DCD Outcomes

- Despite periods of hypotension and warm ischemia, DCD outcomes are mixed but generally acceptable
- Concerns for increased biliary strictures and worse long-term graft survival
- More modern assessment supports comparable outcomes to brain-dead donors with appropriate donor selection
- Use of normothermic regional perfusion and normothermic machine perfusion is believed to reduce ischemic cholangiopathy

## Injuries During Liver Procurement

- Occur in roughly **20% to 30%** of organ donors
- Broken down into:
  - Parenchymal injuries
  - Vascular injuries
  - Bile duct injuries
- Most common major injury: aberrant hepatic artery ligation and division

## Aberrant Hepatic Artery Injury

- Occurs by failure to recognize a replaced or accessory right or left hepatic artery during hilar dissection
- Or by unintentional division during organ removal
- Hiatt et al. 1000 donor case series:
  - Replaced/accessory right: ~10%
  - Similar frequency for left replaced/accessory arteries
  - 3% had dual replacement arteries

## Vascular Injury Significance

- Despite lower frequency of nontraditional vascular anatomy, hilar replaced left and right arteries represent **two-thirds of all vascular injuries** during procurement
- Injuries are serious because segments of the liver are not perfused during recovery
- Usually require reconstruction on the back table before reimplantation
- Associated with a high rate of early HAT (30%) and subsequent need for re-transplantation

## Parenchymal Injuries

- Most common form of minor liver injury during graft removal
- Often can be treated with:
  - Topical hemostatic agents
  - Cautery
  - Liver stitch
- Can also occur during graft implantation
- Associated with long operative times and increased blood loss
- Do **not** have an impact on long-term graft function

## Bile Duct Injuries

- More infrequent complication
- Can be due to stripping vascular supply or cutting the duct too short
- Managed by Roux-en-Y biliary reconstruction
- Typically not associated with graft loss

## Donor Factors Contributing to Morbidity

- Prolonged cold-ischemia time
  - Grafts with >12 hours of cold ischemia at increased risk for graft loss and complications
- Macrosteatosis >30% associated with poor early graft function
- High BMI donors used less commonly
- Bedside biopsy and procurement biopsy can improve high BMI donor liver utilization
- Macrosteatosis >30% prevalent in only 21% of high BMI donors

## Technical Challenges with High BMI Donors

- Visceral adipose tissue makes liver procurement more challenging and time consuming
- Some authors suggest the en bloc method of removing abdominal organs with back-table dissection
- Regardless of technique, attention to detail and identification of appropriate anatomy helps avoid graft procurement injury

## Perioperative Management of Coagulopathy and Bleeding

- Patients with ESLD come to the OR with a spectrum of coagulation abnormalities
- Adaptive changes in coagulation: combination of pro- and anticoagulants with derangements of fibrinolysis
- Individuals prone to both massive hemorrhage or life-threatening thrombosis
- Compounded by portal hypertension and adhesions from prior abdominal surgery

## Challenges from Prior Abdominal Surgery

- Patients with previous operations are at particular risk
- Prolonged lysis of adhesions may greatly increase operation duration
- Creates additional raw surface areas for bleeding
- Leads to derangements in temperature and fluid homeostasis
- Net result: worsening coagulopathy → vicious cycle

## Preoperative Assessment of Coagulation

- Can help guide anesthesia and surgical team for patients at risk of massive bleeding
- Attenuating blood loss has been proposed to improve long-term outcomes after LT
- Blood loss during surgery has incremental increase in postoperative complications and decrease in graft survival
- Blood utilization in LT is under close scrutiny

## Historical Blood Utilization

- Early report from Starzl in the 1980s:
  - 3% to 9% of all blood products in the Pittsburgh central blood bank were used for LT
- Proposed threshold for excessive bleeding in LT: more than **10 units of red blood cells (RBCs)**
- Viscoelastic testing (TEG and ROTEM) used to predict massive transfusion
- TEG maximum amplitude associated with massive transfusion with higher performance than INR and MELD
- ROTEM outperforms conventional assays in predicting nonsurgical bleeding after LT

## Preemptive Treatment of Coagulopathy

- Often not indicated for mild to moderate derangements in coagulation
- Platelets believed to be rapidly sequestered by the spleen based on historic data
- Plasma transfusions can exacerbate venous hypertension and paradoxically increase bleeding
- Early use of prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) associated with reduced blood loss
  - PCC corrects INR without requiring plasma volume
  - Associated with life-threatening thrombotic complications — conservative use advised

## Intraoperative Planning for High-Risk Patients

- Regardless of institution's treatment plan, high-risk patients warrant careful intraoperative planning
- Mobilization of the blood bank
- Use of cell saver for autologous blood transfusion

## Hypercoagulable Profile in LT Recipients

- Evolving measurements of coagulation have revealed a cohort of LT recipients with a hypercoagulable profile
- Cirrhosis is an independent risk factor for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in hospitalized patients
- NASH associated with an even higher risk of thrombotic complications
- Conventional coagulation measurements do not capture this hypercoagulable state in LT

## Thromboelastography and HAT Risk

- Elevated preoperative TEG maximum amplitude (clot strength) associated with a **5-fold risk of early HAT**
- This unmeasured hypercoagulability associated with HAT was attributed to the operating surgeon
- No guidelines on managing preoperative hypercoagulability in LT recipients
- Authors have adopted intraoperative heparin bolus after hepatic artery anastomosis in selected recipients
  - Particularly LDLT with PSC or HCC and high clot strength (MA >65) on early intraoperative TEG

## Bloodless LT and TIPS

- Improvements in surgical techniques and better patient selection → LT without need for blood transfusion in selected patients
- Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) can significantly lower portal hypertension preoperatively
- May help reduce blood loss during transplantation
- However, misplaced TIPS in the vena cava or portal vein can be a life-threatening complication
- TIPS removal can be difficult and may lead to massive hemorrhage
- Temporary portocaval shunts can decompress portal circulation during hepatectomy

## Managing Severe Portal Hypertension and Coagulopathy

- Infusion of fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate, and antifibrinolytic agents can help with hemostasis
- These modalities cannot supplant sound surgical technique with adequate control of all bleeding sites
- Essential to have good communication with anesthesiology team
- Authors use a scoring system to communicate with anesthesia:
  - When a patient warrants coagulation assessment for moderate coagulopathy
  - Empiric transfusions for uncontrolled coagulopathy

## Transition in Hemostasis Management

- Important transition occurs when native liver is removed and new graft undergoes early reperfusion
- Recipients develop a hyperfibrinolytic state (excessive clot degradation from elevated t-PA) when native liver is removed
- After reperfusion, majority of patients correct their fibrinolytic state
- Likely due to rapid clearance of t-PA by the liver
- t-PA half-life: 5 minutes in humans due to multiple hepatic endothelial receptors

## Lack of t-PA Clearance After Reperfusion

- Lack of clearance of t-PA after graft reperfusion can be associated with massive bleeding
- Exacerbated by metabolic disturbances
- In these scenarios, antifibrinolytics may be of value to improve hemostasis control
- Bleeding after reperfusion may be related to poor initial graft function
- Also related to release of heparin and heparin-like substances from the graft
- Protamine administration rarely used; heparin effect often mediated by plasma transfusion

## Temporary Intra-abdominal Tamponade

- When medical strategies fail to halt reperfusion fibrinolysis
- Most conservative management: temporary intra-abdominal tamponade with laparotomy packs
- Temporary vacuum-pack closure with plans for subsequent reexploration
- If graft functions well and patient responds to core temperature warming and continued resuscitation, packs usually can be removed within 24 to 48 hours
- Prophylaxis against intra-abdominal sepsis with parenteral antibiotics: unproven benefit but may be prudent in immunosuppressed patients

## Post-Reperfusion Management

- After reperfusion in grafts with good function, de-escalation of hemostatic blood products is warranted
- TEG and ROTEM have comparable performance for monitoring coagulation during LT
- Routine use associated with using less plasma during surgery in RCTs
- Not associated with reduction in RBC transfusions
- Almost all LT recipients develop inhibition of their fibrinolytic system 2 hours after reperfusion

## Fibrinolysis Shutdown

- Persists beyond postoperative day 1 in the majority of LT patients
- With lack of capacity to break down endogenous clots, essential not to overtransfuse recipients
- Fibrinolysis shutdown associated with decreased graft survival and postoperative thrombotic complications
- Platelet transfusions associated with decreased survival after transplantation
  - Attributed to development of postoperative lung injury

## Postoperative Transfusion Guidance

- Decision to transfuse hemostatic blood products should be guided predominantly by clinical judgement
- Laboratory confirmation of stable hemoglobin levels
- Failure to identify coagulopathy will result in a return trip to the OR
- No definitive thresholds for transfusions

## Authors' Transfusion Thresholds (Table)

| Parameter | Threshold |
|---|---|
| Target hemoglobin | 10 (to promote platelet margination) |
| Platelet transfusion | Absolute platelet count <30,000, or TEG MA 50 with dropping hemoglobin |
| Plasma transfusion | TEG R time >10 minutes or INR >2 with dropping hemoglobin |
| Cryoprecipitate | Clauss fibrinogen <100 or TEG angle <55 if hemoglobin is dropping |
| Return to OR | >6 hours of RBC postoperative bleeding |

## Early Allograft Dysfunction and Primary Nonfunction

- Numerous conditions can interfere with initial function of the allograft:
  - Donor-related factors
  - Procurement-related factors
  - Recipient-related factors
- Donor-related factors affecting graft function adversely:
  - Hemodynamic instability
  - Poor nutritional status
  - Extremes of age
  - Drug toxicity
  - Steatosis

## Spectrum of Graft Dysfunction

- Range from early allograft dysfunction (EAD) to the most extreme, primary nonfunction (PNF)
- Patients with PNF require relisting for transplantation
- Mortality rate can be as high as **50%** even after re-transplantation
- PNF occurs in 2% to 6% of LTs
- Patients do not retain hepatic function → clinical manifestations often not subtle

## Clinical Manifestations of PNF

- Altered mental status
- Persistent acidosis
- Hypoglycemia
- Coagulopathy
- Hemodynamic instability

## Risk Factors for PNF

- Steatosis of the donor liver (major risk factor)
- Female donor
- Older donor
- Long cold and warm ischemia times
- Laboratory values concerning for PNF:
  - Serum transaminase levels >8000 IU/L within first 24 to 48 hours
  - Diminished bile and urine output

## Predicting Graft Function

- Postoperative trends in serum bilirubin and INR are the most reliable predictors of graft function and outcome
- Laboratory studies drawn immediately after surgery serve as baseline
- Serum bilirubin and INR should plateau and then trend toward normalization within days with good graft function
- Any increase in serum bilirubin and INR portends a worse prognosis and may represent PNF
- Elevated INR that neither increases nor decreases may suggest primary graft dysfunction

## Biomarkers and Clinical Assessment

- No definitive test can differentiate slow graft function that will improve from PNF
- Clinical assessment helpful in identifying patients with graft dysfunction or nonfunction:
  - Resolution of hepatic encephalopathy
  - Adequate urine production
  - Absence of metabolic acidosis

## Metabolic Alkalosis as an Indicator

- In patients who received significant quantities of blood products, development of metabolic alkalosis may be a sensitive indicator of early graft function
- Based on ability of liver graft to process citrate in administered blood products to bicarbonate
- Failure to metabolize citrate to bicarbonate may reflect early allograft dysfunction

## Progressive Graft Dysfunction Management

- Early consideration for relisting with higher urgency (status 1) may be the only way to salvage the patient
- Similar to patients with acute liver failure and hypoglycemia, death usually occurs within hours
- Aggressive metabolic supportive measures needed to:
  - Prevent bleeding complications
  - Maintain acid-base status
  - Prevent permanent brain injury from cerebral edema or coagulopathic bleed

## Early Allograft Dysfunction (EAD)

- Broader term capturing LT recipients who do not necessarily require re-transplantation but have less favorable outcomes
- Occurs in roughly **25%** of recipients
- Associated with up to a **7-fold increased risk of early graft loss**
- Associated with **10-fold risk of mortality** after transplant
- Clinical gestalt for slow graft function made after reperfusion
- Time frame for diagnosis with objective laboratory data commonly calculated at 7 days after LT

## Risk Factors for EAD in Adults

- High levels of macrosteatosis
- Donor location
- Donor weight
- DCD donor
- Recipient obesity
- Recipient HCC
- Severity of postreperfusion syndrome
- Warm and cold ischemia time
- Operative time
- Amount of transfused fresh frozen plasma

## Model for Early Allograft Function (MEAF)

- Newer definitions of EAD include a continuous variable termed MEAF
- Grades severity of dysfunction, ranges from 1 to 10
- Based on postoperative day 3 laboratory values
- Each increase in MEAF score associated with progressively lower graft survival time
- Numerous other definitions of EAD exist with variances in performance
- Authors prefer the Olthoff et al. definition due to simplicity and agreement between LDLT and cadaveric liver recipients

## Graft Size and SFSS in LDLT

- In LDLT, graft size was an initial concern for development of EAD
- SFSS can be a significant cause of live-donor graft dysfunction and graft loss
- Additional evidence suggests importance of pressure and flow as major contributors rather than size alone
- Graft to body weight ratio of 0.8 can be transplanted successfully
- Key prognostic factor for good graft function with smaller livers: portal systemic gradient <15 mm Hg
- EAD serves as a better predictor for long-term graft function than small graft size

## Risk Factors for LDLT EAD

- Increasing age of the donor
- BMI of the donor
- Left liver grafts
- Enlarged spleen in the recipients

## Treatment of EAD — Randomized Controlled Trial

- One successful RCT targeting EAD
- 65 patients randomized to steroids or standard of care if they met EAD definition (bilirubin >10 on postoperative day 7)
- Steroid intervention group: methylprednisolone IV once daily for 5 days
- Both arms received 250 mg oral ursodeoxycholic acid three times a day
- At end of 2 weeks: treatment arm had lower alkaline phosphatase levels, lower bilirubin levels, and shorter hospital length of stay
- No reported increased rates of infections or other steroid-related complications

## Vascular Complications — Overview

- Major source of morbidity and graft loss in LT patients
- Especially those who receive live-donor grafts
- Arterial complications, of which HAT is most common, account for 64% to 82% of vascular complications
- Overall incidence of HAT: 1.6% to 8% in adult series
- Can be 15% to 26% in pediatric patients
- Incidence in LDLT varies widely — influenced by graft type, surgeon experience, donor anatomy

## Hepatic Artery Thrombosis — Risk Factors

- Donor CMV positivity in a CMV-negative recipient
- Prolonged operating time
- Redo LT
- Arterial conduit
- Variant arterial anatomy
- Low surgical volume
- Preoperative transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) associated with hepatic artery complications but not specific to HAT

## Early vs Late HAT

- Time cutoff for early HAT remains an academic debate (7 to 100 days)
- UNOS policy defines early HAT as lasting <7 days with AST >3000 and INR >2.5 or acidosis (arterial pH <7.3 or lactate >4) to qualify for status 1A
- Early HAT of <14 days regardless of other factors qualifies recipients as MELD 40
- Attempt at revascularization should be conducted in setting of early HAT because salvage is possible
- Alternative is re-transplantation, which uses another organ

## Late HAT

- Typically presents as a biliary complication or identified incidentally on imaging
- Bilomas are the most common presenting symptom
- Can be salvaged with percutaneous drainage and antibiotics
- Lower frequency than early HAT
- Tends to have better prognosis with lower rate of requiring re-transplantation
- Asymptomatic individuals can often be observed and followed for biliary complications
- Risk factors: CMV infection and variant arterial anatomy

## Diagnosis of HAT

- Doppler ultrasound (US) is the best screening method
- Should be used liberally in the first 2 weeks after transplantation with any change in graft function or significant elevation in bilirubin or transaminases
- Collateral blood flow through gastroduodenal artery can result in false-negative result
- Care must be taken to establish arterial flow within the hepatic parenchyma
- Confirmation by celiac arteriography, multiphase CT, or operative exploration
- Failure to make rapid diagnosis can result in hepatic necrosis and graft loss

## Figure 111.1 — Hepatic Artery Thrombosis

![Hepatic artery thrombosis](figure111_1.png)

- Patient experienced rapid increase in serum transaminases in early postoperative period
- Ultrasound could not locate an intrahepatic arterial signal
- Celiac arteriography shows left gastric and splenic arterial flow and fails to show any contrast in the liver
- Consistent with intimal dissection of the entire common hepatic artery
- T-tube within the common bile duct is visible

## Intimal Dissection of the Recipient Hepatic Artery

- Common cause of intraoperative HAT
- Dissection down to the origin of the celiac axis
- Immediate reconstruction with a donor iliac allograft is indicated
- Under no circumstances should the patient leave the OR without a completely revascularized graft
- When donor iliac allograft is unusable or unavailable, autogenous saphenous vein graft should be used
- Rarely, artificial conduit made from Dacron or expanded polytetrafluoroethylene can be used

## Figure 111.2 — Hepatic Artery Reconstruction

![Hepatic artery reconstruction](figure111_2.png)

- With early diagnosis of HAT, immediate reconstruction with a donor iliac artery allograft can be performed
- In this case, the iliac artery graft is anastomosed between the infrarenal aorta and liver allograft common hepatic artery

## Clinical Presentation of Postoperative HAT

- Ranges from completely asymptomatic patient with minimal alterations in liver function
- To critically ill patient with fulminant hepatic necrosis
- More common presentation: postoperative biliary complications
  - Leaks
  - Stricture formation

## Treatment of HAT

- Treatment in early postoperative period is the same whether symptoms are present or not
- Rapid reestablishment of arterial inflow should be attempted
- Generally requires urgent operation with arterial reconstruction using donor iliac artery allograft or autogenous graft material
- Some authors have attempted thrombolysis using fibrinolytics followed by stent placement
  - Not common practice; durable successful results remain limited
- Most often, hepatic artery intimal dissection is not amenable to thrombolytic therapy
- Attempts at systemic thrombolysis waste valuable time and resources and worsen outcome
- Majority of patients (50%–70%) will ultimately require re-transplantation

## Portal Vein Thrombosis/Stenosis

- PVT observed before surgery was previously considered an absolute contraindication to orthotopic LT (OLT)
- No longer precludes successful LT
- Presence may substantially increase surgical complexity and perioperative morbidity
- Depending on patient population, PVT found in 5% to 25% of LT recipients
- Severity of thrombosis ranges greatly between patients
- Portal vein inflow is essential for successful LT
- Imaging with duplex or CT before implant is an invaluable resource for intraoperative planning

## Yerdel Classification of PVT (Table)

| Grade | Description |
|---|---|
| 1 | Less than 50% PVT |
| 2 | Greater than 50% with minimal superior mesenteric vein (SMV) obstruction |
| 3 | 100% PVT |
| 4 | 100% PVT with SMV thrombosis |

## Surgical Management by Yerdel Grade

- Grade 1 and 2: intraoperative thrombectomy can be used
- Grade 3: a jump graft can be used
- Grade 4: relative contraindication to transplant unless bypass is achievable to a nonmesenteric venous source
- Reconstruction of the portal can be accomplished using a donor iliac vein allograft anastomosed between the SMV and liver allograft portal vein
- Successful reconstructed inflow for grade 4 reported in >75% of patients but prone to stenosis
- Living-donor grafts with relatively short portal vein segments can be difficult to reconstruct
- Some institutions consider PVT an absolute contraindication to LDLT

## Post-Transplant PVT

- Rare complication that can occur in the immediate postoperative period
- Usually for technical reasons:
  - Incomplete thrombectomy
  - Twisting of the anastomosis
- Early PVT has a poor prognosis with mortality rate of 50%
- Predominantly because of later complications after attempted repair
- Risk factors for early PVT: postoperative platelet transfusions, RBC transfusion, and PVT before transplant

## Late PVT

- Observed several months to years after transplantation
- Usually results from intimal hyperplasia with gradual cavernous transformation with collaterals
- High index of suspicion needed to make the diagnosis
- Accumulation of ascites, splenomegaly, or presence of varices after transplantation should prompt investigation
- Early thrombosis best treated with reoperation, thrombectomy, and systemic anticoagulation
- Partial PVT can alternatively be approached with systemic heparinization and serial ultrasounds
- Late thrombosis and portal vein stenosis increasingly treated successfully with interventional procedures

## Inferior Vena Cava Obstruction

- Rare complication occurring in 1% of patients after LT
- Historically, donor IVC anastomosed with suprahepatic and infrahepatic IVC
- Piggyback transplantation: anastomosis of donor suprahepatic IVC to confluence of recipient middle and left hepatic veins, leaving recipient IVC in situ
- Piggyback technique associated with reduced blood loss, shorter warm ischemia times, and lower rates of acute kidney injury
- Concerns for increased rate of outflow obstruction due to anastomotic strictures or kinking at hepatic veins
- Higher frequencies in LDLT and pediatric LTs

## Outflow Obstruction Management

- Early after transplant, high outflow obstruction can be confused with increased central venous pressure (CVP) due to high volume resuscitation
- Manifests as DGF, ascites, and peripheral edema
- Nonanatomic source of outflow obstruction treated with diuretics, targeting CVP below 11
- When CVP ruled out, evaluate with venography of the vena cava with segmental pressures
- Gradient >10 mm Hg with clinical symptoms of lower extremity edema, ascites, and slow hepatic function can warrant intervention (often angioplasty)
- Later-onset anastomotic stenosis treated with repeat angioplasty and stenting with durable long-term results

## IVC Thrombosis

- Additional cause of outflow obstruction
- Treatment usually depends on the cause
- Direct surgical removal is difficult in a critically ill patient
- Requires extensive mobilization of the right colon and small bowel mesentery
- Nonoperative management successful in authors' experience and that reported by others
- Conservative management algorithm using invasive radiologic procedures and systemic anticoagulation can treat this complication satisfactorily
- Thrombolytic therapy can be adjunctive in resolving "fresh" thrombus formation

## High-Grade Venous Outflow Obstruction

- In some cases, cannot be corrected
- TIPS may be used as a bridge to mediate ascites and bleeding complications for re-transplantation candidates
- Use of TIPS posttransplantation associated with accelerated decline in hepatic function
- Not a durable therapy — patient will progress to need another LT

## Veno-Occlusive Disease / Sinusoidal Obstruction Syndrome (VOD/SOS)

- Additional cause of symptoms that can mimic outflow obstruction
- Believed related to acute rejection and drug toxicity
- Often occurs months after transplant
- Originally described in bone marrow transplants
- More recently identified as a rare cause of liver failure after transplantation
- Diagnosed via liver biopsy — demonstrates fibrous obliteration of the small hepatic veins
- Most effective treatment in bone marrow patients: Defibrotide
- Success with LT recipients not as clear; medication activates fibrinolytic system and poses bleeding risk
- Alternative strategies: steroids, increasing immunosuppression, TIPS as last-line therapy

## Biliary Complications — Overview

- Previously considered the Achilles heel of LT
- Improvements in operative technique have greatly reduced these complications
- Bile duct obstruction and leaks are the cause of approximately half of all technical failures after LT
- Require reoperation in 10% to 20% of patients
- Recipients of living-donor grafts have incidence of biliary complications approximately **two times higher** than cadaveric grafts
- HAT is associated with biliary complications

## Biliary Leaks

- Reported incidence varies widely, from 10% to 50%
- Observed most often at site of choledochal anastomosis or choledochal T-tube insertion site
- Leaks at insertion site observed most frequently at tube removal
- Occur in as many as 25% to 40% of patients
- Most can be managed conservatively with short course of analgesics and antibiotics
- To minimize risk, many surgeons prefer not to place stents

## Authors' Stenting Practice

- Rather than conventional T-tube, authors stent choledochal anastomosis with a 5 French pediatric feeding tube
- Placed through the cystic duct stump
- Secured with a hemorrhoidal band and polydioxanone suture (PDS)
- In theory, hemorrhoidal band obliterates lumen of preformed tract at stent removal
- Usually removed 6 to 8 weeks postoperatively
- Anastomotic leaks in early postoperative period related to technical errors, tension at anastomotic site, or ischemic necrosis after HAT

## Biliary Leak Diagnosis and Treatment

- Bile ducts of living-donor or split-liver grafts can be reconstructed with duct-to-duct (choledochocholedochostomy) or Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy
- Leak rate similar in both types of reconstructions
- Signs and symptoms: bilious fluid in drains, abdominal or shoulder pain, increased serum bilirubin, nausea, vomiting, fever
- Diagnosis confirmed by cholangiography, ERC, or PTC
- Authors favor ERC — treatment with endoscopic stent placement without risk of indwelling transhepatic catheters
- Large biliary leaks with bile collections adjacent to liver require percutaneous drainage

## Management of Large Leaks

- Larger leaks and those associated with ischemic necrosis require surgical revision with Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy
- Development of early postoperative leaks is associated with late stricture formation
- Lifelong surveillance by the surgeon is warranted

## Biliary Stricture or Obstruction

- Occurs in approximately 7% to 15% of patients after LT
- Site of obstruction aids in determining cause
- Anastomotic stricture accounts for 50% of obstruction cases
- Can occur early (secondary to edema) or later (as a result of compromised blood supply)
- Biliary strictures usually present within weeks but may occur years after transplantation
- Two types: anastomotic and nonanastomotic
- Nonanastomotic obstruction can be caused by bile duct ischemia or sludge and debris

## Diagnosis of Biliary Stricture

- Suggested by obstructive pattern on routine liver function tests
- Patients typically seen with constitutional symptoms: rigor, fever, headache, fatigue
- Occasionally present with severe symptoms of cholangitis and sepsis
- Diagnosis can be difficult — mild signs may reflect acute rejection, HAT, CMV infection, or recurrent disease
- Diagnostic studies include abdominal US, cholangiography, and liver biopsy

## Figure 111.3 — Biliary Stricture

![Biliary stricture](figure111_3.png)

- Patient had a previously created Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy and now has an anastomotic stricture
- Note the dilated intrahepatic ducts
- Percutaneous access of the Roux-en-Y limb affords ability to make diagnosis and treat with balloon dilation
- Using this technique, placement of transhepatic catheters is avoided

## Causes of Biliary Stricture

- Most common site: biliary anastomosis
- Technical error during reconstruction is an important causative factor
- Patency of hepatic artery should be assessed, particularly in pediatric recipients
- Other implicated factors:
  - ABO incompatibility
  - Prolonged preservation times
  - Recurrent rejection
  - Viral infections
  - Recurrence of primary ductal disease (up to 50% of recipients at long-term follow-up)

## Figure 111.4 — Nonanastomotic Biliary Stricture

![Nonanastomotic biliary stricture](figure111_4.png)

- Nonanastomotic biliary stricture (arrow) observed from ischemic injury to a liver graft
- Patient received a liver from a donor who died of cardiac death rather than brain death
- DCD is an attempt to expand the organ donor pool
- Such grafts are more prone to ischemic injury problems such as bile duct stricture

## Biliary Reconstruction After LDLT

- By Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy or duct-to-duct anastomosis
- Anastomotic leak or stricture generally **two times more common** after LDLT versus cadaveric LT
- Nonanastomotic strictures (NAS) can occur in hilar region or intrahepatically
- Thrombosis of hepatic artery or one of its branches should be suspected
- NAS also reported with chronic ductopenic rejection, ABO blood group incompatibility, and ischemia-reperfusion injury
- Especially in grafts from DCD donors

## Treatment of Biliary Stricture

- After appropriate fluid resuscitation and antibiotic coverage, ERC recommended to confirm diagnosis and implement treatment with immediate stenting if possible
- Failure to cross stricture through endoscopic means requires PTC or surgical revision with Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy
- Intrahepatic strictures best treated with percutaneous balloon dilation
- Rarely, long-term stents needed to achieve satisfactory outcome

## Ischemic Cholangiopathy

- Represents a spectrum of NAS in LT that tends to be diffuse
- Main causes:
  - Ischemia reperfusion injury
  - Immune-mediated injury
  - Bile salt injury
- Major risk factors: HAT and DCD donors
- Broken down into clinical and subclinical cholangiopathy based on laboratory assessment and cholangiography
- Subclinical cholangiopathy can often be observed with minimal effect on long-term outcomes

## Types of Ischemic Cholangiopathy

- Within clinical cholangiopathy score, a rapidly progressive form associated with necrosis warrants urgent re-transplantation
- Additional more indolent forms:
  - Multifocal progressive stenosis
  - Centrifugal progressive stenosis
- Last form of clinical cholangiopathy: hilar confluence abnormalities
- Combination of laboratory abnormalities and cholangiogram abnormalities associated with marked reduction in graft survival at 5 years

## Management of Ischemic Cholangiopathy

- No effective treatments aside from treating focal strictures
- Can be managed on repeat interventions to enable patient to avoid transplantation
- Best strategy is to avoid ischemic cholangiopathy altogether
- Proposed: tPA treatment in DCD donors — demonstrated reduction in ischemic cholangiopathy and improved graft survival
- Newer strategies: machine perfusion of high-risk donors
- Promising results in reducing biliary complications after LT in several clinical trials

## Renal Dysfunction

- Observed to some degree in almost every patient who undergoes LT
- Early renal dysfunction usually characterized by period of oliguria with transient increase in serum creatinine
- Can also manifest as anuria with acute renal failure
- Risk factors: preexisting renal dysfunction and primary graft nonfunction
- In patients with normal preoperative serum creatinine and good initial graft function, usual mechanism is prerenal azotemia
- Secondary to periods of hypotension and hypovolemia during operative procedure

## Calcineurin Inhibitor Nephrotoxicity

- Additional insult from administration of nephrotoxic agents
- Especially calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs) cyclosporine and tacrolimus
- Renal failure induced by CNIs occurs in approximately 5% of transplanted patients
- Etiology of renal failure can be multifactorial
- Long-term exposure (dose/time) to CNIs is a clear risk factor
- Increasing interest in automatic dose reduction in patients many years after transplantation and those showing signs of progressive renal dysfunction

## Sirolimus and Renal Sparing

- Another strategy: substitution of immunosuppressive regimen with drugs that do not cause renal dysfunction
- Mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitors (sirolimus, everolimus)
- Sirolimus (rapamycin) is a macrocyclic antibiotic originally developed as anticandidal and antitumor agent
- Often used for renal sparing
- Disadvantage: increased risk for dyslipidemia and impaired wound healing
- Impaired wound healing may be related to alterations in VEGF
- May explain apparent benefit of sirolimus in reducing cancer formation

## Sirolimus and HAT Risk

- Sirolimus associated with early HAT after LT
- Manufacturer recommends waiting at least 4 weeks after transplantation before initiating therapy

## Post-Transplantation Renal Failure Requiring Dialysis

- Uncommon unless patient has preexisting hepatorenal syndrome or severe hypotension and hemorrhage during surgery resulting in acute tubular necrosis
- Authors' experience: dialysis best performed with continuous venovenous hemodialysis using a dedicated, large-bore, double-lumen venous access device
- Recovery of normal renal function usually achieved within 2 weeks if no other metabolic stress

## Fluid and Electrolyte Disturbances

- Universal after LT
- Preoperative protein-calorie malnutrition and ESLD lead to derangements in total body water and electrolyte balance
- Worsened initially by metabolic stress of surgery and massive fluid and blood-product resuscitation
- Rapidity of recovery depends largely on patient's renal and liver allograft function postoperatively
- For patient with stable postoperative renal and liver graft function, minimal metabolic manipulation required

## Metabolic Alkalosis After LT

- Early development of metabolic alkalosis secondary to metabolism of citrate in blood products is a favorable sign of graft function
- Can be serious if alkaemia develops
- Judicious replacement of chloride in the form of normal saline or hydrogen chloride is warranted

## Managing Fluid and Electrolyte Derangements

- Excess total body water and excess sodium best treated with gentle diuresis with furosemide
- Careful repletion of potassium — must be monitored closely with medications such as tacrolimus (tends to increase serum potassium)
- Derangements in serum calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus common in patients with cirrhosis
- Levels should be repleted to avoid neurologic, skeletal, and cardiac muscle dysfunction

## Acute Cellular Rejection

- In early days of LT, importance of rejection was overshadowed by technical complications
- As surgical technique evolved with concomitant improvement in graft preservation, rejection has taken on greater clinical importance
- Acute cellular rejection: acute deterioration in allograft function associated with specific histologic changes
- Changes include mixed inflammatory cell infiltrate, predominantly lymphocytes
- Involves portal triads and disrupts biliary, hepatic artery, and portal venous endothelia

## Incidence of Acute Rejection

- Approximately 45% (range, 24%–80%), depending on series reported
- Acute rejection has little to no impact on mortality
- Significant morbidity results in increased hospitalization and higher overall costs
- In early stage, most patients are asymptomatic
- Variety of clinical signs and symptoms may develop: fever, abdominal pain, malaise, fatigue, poor appetite

## Laboratory Indicators of Acute Rejection

- Earliest laboratory indicator: elevated bilirubin level
- May be associated with modest increase in alkaline phosphatase and transaminase levels
- Prothrombin time (PT) and serum albumin levels usually unaffected
- Laboratory measurements neither sensitive nor specific for acute cellular rejection
- Liver histology from percutaneous biopsy remains the standard for diagnosis

## Treatment of Acute Cellular Rejection (Banff Score)

| Rejection Severity | RAI Score | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Mild | RAI <4 | Increasing calcineurin inhibitor |
| Moderate | RAI 4–6 | High-dose pulse corticosteroids |
| Severe | RAI >7 | High-dose pulse corticosteroids |

- High-dose pulse corticosteroids successful in approximately 80% to 90% of cases

## Induction Immunosuppression

- Use of other induction immunosuppressive agents such as antithymocyte globulin (thymoglobulin) does not improve rates or graft survival rates of LT patients when used as induction agent
- Can be used as an adjunct in steroid-resistant antibody-mediated rejection (AMR)

## Chronic Rejection

- Unlike acute rejection, chronic rejection in LT is associated with reduced graft survival
- No effective treatments
- Occurs in roughly 10% of all LTs
- Chronic ductopenic rejection rarely occurs in first 2 months after LT
- Defined as loss of bile ducts in more than 50% of portal tracts (when 20 or more portal tracts available for evaluation)
- Diagnosed on basis of histologic criteria
- Early ductopenia associated with high mortality rate

## Chronic Rejection — Additional Features

- Arteriopathy described, affecting large and medium-sized arteries
- Characterized by foam cell infiltration of the intima
- Most important manifestation of chronic rejection: ductopenic rejection
- Term used synonymously with histologic description "vanishing bile duct syndrome"
- Only effective treatment is re-transplantation

## Antibody-Mediated Rejection (AMR)

- Rare form of immunologic complication after LT
- Overall rate estimated at 1% of all LTs
- Increased to 5% in patients with positive donor-specific antigen (DSA)
- Diagnosed with C4D-positive stained biopsies
- Treatment: plasmapheresis, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and a B-cell-depleting medication such as rituximab
- Relatively newly appreciated phenomenon in LT
- Ongoing work on long-term outcomes after effective treatments

## AMR — Underdiagnosis Concerns

- Concerns that AMR is underdiagnosed
- Rising DSA level post-transplant could be a cause of occult liver fibrosis over an extended period
- Remains an area of debate
- Standardized treatment based on post-transplant DSA has not been established

## Infection — Overview

- With few exceptions, all transplant patients are committed to lifelong immunosuppressant therapy
- Inadequate immunosuppression can result in graft loss
- Injudicious use of immunosuppression can result in life-threatening infection or PTLD
- Tenuous balance between preventing rejection and minimizing risk for nosocomial and opportunistic infection
- Approximately two-thirds of transplant patients experience at least one episode of serious infection
- Accounts for more than half of observed mortality associated with LT

## Risk Factors for Postoperative Infection

- Donor and recipient viral status
- Underlying medical comorbidities
- Nutritional status
- Prolonged surgery with massive blood loss
- Prolonged ischemia time
- Violation of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract

## Bacterial Infections

- Tend to occur within the first month after LT
- Vary from center to center
- Early risk factors: prolonged operating time, indwelling catheters, biliary obstruction, PVT, poor graft function
- Vascular ischemia, recurrent HCV infection, exposure to resistant organisms, chronic rejection, and hyperglycemia can contribute
- Common gram-negative pathogens: Escherichia coli, Enterobacter, Pseudomonas spp. (found in bile)
- Common gram-positive organisms: Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci, group D streptococci
- Rarely, S. aureus can result in toxic shock syndrome in early postoperative period
- Listeria, Nocardia, and Legionella are uncommon but significant pathogens

## Viral Infections

- Common in immunocompromised patients after transplantation
- Other equally important but less common viral infections:
  - Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)
  - Adenovirus
  - Influenza
  - Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)
- Transplant patients at risk for acquiring viral hepatitis from infected organs, blood transfusions, and illicit drug use

## Cytomegalovirus (CMV)

- Most important infection observed in organ transplant patients
- Asymptomatic in general population; significant potential severity in immunosuppressed transplant recipients
- Most important pathogen in clinical transplantation
- CMV disease usually occurs 30 to 50 days after transplantation
- Clinical manifestations: fever, malaise, arthralgia, leukopenia and thrombocytopenia, hepatitis, interstitial pneumonitis, enterocolitis, disseminated disease

## CMV Disease vs CMV Infection

- Differentiation is clinically important
- CMV disease: histologically evident invasive CMV infection or positive CMV culture from deep tissue specimens (liver biopsy, endoscopic mucosal biopsy or brushing, bronchoscopic mucosal biopsy or brushing) in setting of clinical manifestation
- Positive blood, body fluid, or serologic tests insufficient to establish diagnosis of CMV disease
- Liver biopsy with immunostaining using monoclonal antibody against CMV antigen enables early diagnosis
- Common histologic findings: hepatocyte necrosis, parenchymal microabscesses, magenta-colored intranuclear inclusion surrounded by clear halo ("owl's eye nucleus")

## CMV Risk Factors and Treatment

- Risk factors for CMV disease:
  - Seronegative recipient who received organ from seropositive donor
  - Use of anti-lymphocyte antibody therapy (particularly OKT3)
  - Re-transplantation
- Level of immunosuppressive therapy influences manifestation of CMV infection
- Chronic CMV infection with persistent replication within hepatocytes associated with cholestatic hepatitis and vanishing bile duct syndrome
- Treatment: reduction of immunosuppressive regimen, particularly tapering corticosteroid dose
- IV ganciclovir mainstay of therapy — safe and effective for prophylaxis and treatment
- Foscarnet alternative in ganciclovir resistance — less well tolerated, nephrotoxic

## CMV Prophylaxis

- Prophylaxis using oral and IV ganciclovir after transplantation has been effective
- Other regimens (IV ganciclovir plus oral acyclovir for 3 months, or oral acyclovir alone) less successful
- Oral valganciclovir as effective as IV ganciclovir for prevention and treatment of mild CMV infection
- Most transplant centers switched to prophylactic regimens ranging from 3 to 6 months of daily oral treatment (450 or 900 mg depending on renal function)
- Side effects minimal; leukopenia can occur
- Late-onset CMV disease remains a potential problem, especially in patients on higher doses of immunosuppression and high-risk groups (CMV D+/R−)

## Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)

- HSV seropositivity present in most patients undergoing LT
- Postoperative HSV infection usually related to immunosuppression-induced reactivation
- Usually manifests as mild mucocutaneous oral or genital disease that responds to acyclovir
- Prompt recognition important to prevent progression to lethal disseminated disease or fulminant hepatitis
- Fulminant hepatitis can involve coagulopathy, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and death
- Graft involvement diagnosed by characteristic histologic picture on liver biopsy

## Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)

- Belongs to the herpes family
- Infection in transplant patient characterized by mononucleosis-like syndrome
- Differs from normal host by absence of heterophil antibody response and infrequency of pharyngitis or splenomegaly
- Clinical significance related to its role in pathogenesis of PTLD
- Development of PTLD thought to reflect unrestricted proliferation of B cells stimulated by EBV infection

## Opportunistic Infections — Fungal

- Incidence of clinically significant fungal infection: 20% to 25% in LT recipients
- Risk factors: poor nutrition status, re-transplantation, bacterial infection with prolonged antibiotic use, high doses of immunosuppression, biliary reconstruction using Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy
- Invasive fungal infection occurs in 1% to 3% of LT patients
- Associated with high mortality rate

## Risk Factors for Invasive Fungal Infection

- Operative time >11 hours
- Re-transplant
- Creatinine >3.0
- CMV infection
- MELD >30
- Fulminant hepatic failure
- Prolonged ICU stay
- Retrospective data support prophylactic antifungals reducing postoperative invasive fungal infections
- Authors' institution: high-risk patients started on prophylactic Eraxis at time of surgery until hospital discharge

## Fungal Infection Diagnosis and Mortality

- If suspicion of invasive fungal infection is high, every effort should be made to obtain histologic or culture evidence for early diagnosis
- Emerging evidence supports prophylaxis in combination with early detection and treatment reduces mortality from historic near 100% to less than 20%
- Candida: most common fungal infection
  - Acquired by inhalation and colonizes airways
  - May already be colonized in recipient's biliary tract
- Aspergillus: second most frequent fungal pathogen
  - Angioinvasive, tends to disseminate to CNS
  - Can cause infarcts and cavitation in lungs
  - Incidence ~1% in LT recipients, mortality close to 100% despite adequate treatment

## Cryptococcus and Coccidioidomycosis

- Cryptococcus neoformans usually occurs months to years after transplantation
- Affects approximately 0.25% of LT patients
- Signs and symptoms may be subtle → delayed diagnosis common
- Symptoms: changes in mental status, headache, fever
- One patient presented with CNS lesions and large cavitating thoracic masses requiring operative removal
- Coccidioidomycosis: rare fungal infection endemic to the southwest
- Authors' practice: long-term fluconazole prophylaxis for organ recipients from this region

## Pneumocystis carinii Pneumonia

- Previously a common pathogen in immunocompromised host
- Routine prophylaxis with daily low-dose oral trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) for 6 to 12 months
- Or aerosolized pentamidine in patients intolerant to TMP/SMX
- Incidence has decreased dramatically
- Because prophylaxis is so effective, P. carinii pneumonia has occurred almost exclusively in patients who do not receive prophylaxis
- Given low morbidity of prophylactic regimens, no patient should be excluded

## Legionella pneumophila

- Uncommon cause of pneumonia in patients after LT
- As in normal host, source of legionellosis is usually the water supply
- Traditionally treated with erythromycin
- Quinolones also proven effective
- Advantage of quinolones: no interaction with immunosuppressive agents such as cyclosporine or tacrolimus

## Post-Transplantation Lymphoproliferative Disorder (PTLD)

- Life-threatening complication of chronic immunosuppression
- Strongly associated with replication of EBV in B cells induced by enhanced immunosuppression
- Primarily observed in patients who received more than one course of polyclonal antilymphocyte globulin or monoclonal OKT3
- Association with CMV infection also noted
- Incidence varies from 1% to 3% among LT recipients
- Prognosis depends on histologic characteristics of the tumor

## PTLD — Polyclonal vs Monoclonal

- Polyclonal PTLD: treatable with discontinuation of immunosuppression with relatively low risk of rejection
- Monoclonal PTLD: more difficult to treat and can result in death
- Antibody against CD20 represents a novel approach in treating monoclonal PTLD with favorable outcome

## PTLD — Clinical Presentation

- Fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy with or without tonsillitis
- GI bleeding, perforation, or obstruction
- Hepatocellular dysfunction
- CNS manifestations: seizures, mental status changes, focal neurologic symptoms

## PTLD — Characteristics

- Lymphoproliferative disorders after LT have characteristics distinct from those in general population
- Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: 65% of lymphomas in general population vs 93% in transplant recipients
- Mostly large-cell lymphomas; most are B-cell type
- Extranodal involvement common — occurs in approximately 70% of cases

## PTLD — Treatment

- Polyclonal PTLD: reduction of immunosuppressive medications and antiviral therapy
- Monoclonal PTLD and polyclonal disease not responding to reduced immunosuppression: treated with radiation, chemotherapy, and occasionally surgical resection
- Therapy using monoclonal antibody against CD20 shows promising results for monoclonal PTLD

## Acute Immunosuppressive Drug Toxicity

- Immunosuppression must balance beneficial effects in preventing/reversing rejection against dangers of excess immunosuppression
- Dangers: acute toxicity symptoms, nosocomial infection, lymphoproliferative disorders
- Most common agents: CNIs cyclosporine and tacrolimus, with or without corticosteroids
- Azathioprine used frequently in the past, especially in triple-drug therapy
- Mycophenolate mofetil has essentially replaced azathioprine after liver and kidney transplantation
- After initiation, infection and acute toxicity usually seen early
- Lymphoproliferative disorders and other malignancies are long-term sequelae

## CNI Side Effects

- Side effect profiles of cyclosporine and tacrolimus are similar
- Include GI disturbances, headache, tremor
- Gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism encountered frequently during cyclosporine and corticosteroid treatment
- Glucose intolerance reported more often with tacrolimus than cyclosporine
- Hyperkalemia, hyperuricemia, hypophosphatemia, and hypomagnesemia are manifestations of renal tubular dysfunction
- Usually controlled by adjusting dose according to drug levels

## CNI Nephrotoxicity

- Most clinically significant adverse effect of both drugs
- Manifests as acute azotemia
- Largely reversible after reducing dose and providing adequate hydration
- Occasionally progressive chronic renal disease develops in as many as 5% of patients
- Usually irreversible; may require renal replacement therapy or renal transplantation
- Other renal effects of cyclosporine: chronic tubular dysfunction, rarely hemolytic uremic syndrome

## Mycophenolate Mofetil Side Effects

- GI disturbances (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea)
- May increase certain postoperative infections
- Symptoms not uncommon in early transplant patients
- May be difficult to differentiate cause; drug toxicity usually inferred
- Alternative forms of drug may be helpful, as well as dose modification or discontinuation

## Recurrent Hepatitis B

- In patients with cirrhosis secondary to chronic HBV infection, recurrence rate is approximately 80% to 90% in first year
- Evidenced by signs of viral replication (HBV e-antigen-positive or positive titers of HBV DNA)
- Given almost universal recurrence of HBV antigenemia in early postoperative period, some authors questioned utility of liver replacement
- With advent of hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) and other adjuvant therapies (interferon, lamivudine), transplantation now routinely offered with excellent results

## Recurrent Hepatitis C

- Recurrent HCV infection is universal after LT
- In 90% of patients, HCV can be confirmed on routine biopsy
- Of these, 60% have mild hepatitis
- 30% develop a more severe pattern on histologic examination
- In patients with severe recurrent HCV, cirrhosis develops in 20% within 5 years if untreated
- Advent of improved HCV medications with almost 100% cure rates has significantly improved outlook
- For patients with HCV infection waiting for or having received an LT

## Bone Disease

- Almost all patients who undergo LT have some degree of hepatic osteodystrophy
- Especially those with primary biliary cirrhosis
- Mechanism seems to vary according to underlying disease
- Causes are multifactorial: corticosteroid therapy, bed rest, cholestasis
- Osteoporosis particularly common 3 to 6 months after LT
- By end of first year after transplantation, patients start gaining bone density
- Late improvement probably due to reduction in corticosteroid therapy and resolution of pre-transplantation condition

## Bone Disease — Fractures and Necrosis

- Atraumatic bone fractures more frequent within first 6 months after LT
- Due to extensive bone loss during this period
- Avascular necrosis and vertebral body collapse may also occur
- Especially in those maintained on corticosteroid therapy

## Neuropsychiatric Complications

- Severe neuropsychiatric changes can occur after LT
- Acute neurophysiologic changes associated with fluid and electrolyte shifts during perioperative period
- Anxiety and depression common psychiatric conditions in many transplant patients
- Seizures, altered levels of consciousness, and CNS infections are infrequent but significant causes of morbidity and mortality
- Encephalopathy after LT may be related to poor initial graft function but more often multifactorial
- Metabolic derangements, hypoxia, sedation, and drug interactions all can contribute

## Neuropsychiatric — Immunosuppression Toxicity

- Neurologic signs and symptoms associated with cyclosporine and tacrolimus toxicity: tremors, headaches, seizures
- Can be avoided by close monitoring of drug levels
- High-dose corticosteroids can result in emotional lability or mania
- Any patient with new neuropsychiatric symptoms should have cranial CT scan and lumbar puncture
- To rule out other causes of mental status changes: intracerebral bleeding or infectious etiology

## Hypertension and Hyperlipidemia

- Common sequelae of immunosuppression in post-transplantation period
- Although patient survival improves, consequences have greater importance on long-term prognosis
- Hypertension observed in approximately 70% of LT recipients at 1 year
- Almost 40% of patients manifest metabolic syndrome with diabetes, sustained hypercholesterolemia, and hypertriglyceridemia during same period
- Pathophysiology of post-transplantation hyperlipidemia is complex

## Management of Hyperlipidemia

- Rapamycin immunosuppression does not cause glucose intolerance
- Can lead to hyperlipidemia, problems with wound healing, and mouth ulcers
- Omega-3 fatty acids found in fish oil can reduce hypertriglyceridemia significantly
- Authors' experience: oral supplementation with over-the-counter fish oil capsules providing 1 to 2 g of EPA and DHA
- Shown a dose-response reduction in serum triglycerides
- Most fish oil supplements are 30% to 55% EPA and DHA — multiple capsules may be needed
- Given additional risk of coronary artery and peripheral vascular disease, aggressive therapy with dietary changes, exercise, and medication is indicated

## Conclusion

- LT is a lifesaving treatment modality for patients with ESLD
- Wide range of comorbidities that develop preoperatively contribute significantly to postoperative complications
- Aggressive use of immunosuppression is successful in preventing rejection in many cases
- Therapy can be complicated by development of life-threatening neoplasms

## Conclusion — Recent Trends

- Recent trends favor significant reduction of immunosuppression with time
- Early withdrawal of corticosteroids, once the mainstay of immunosuppressive regimens
- Reduction of immunosuppression in select patients and early withdrawal of steroids have significantly reduced morbidity and life-threatening complications
- Positive outcomes after LT require a multidisciplinary team approach
- Team includes surgeons, transplant coordinators, hepatologists, and internists
- To maintain constant surveillance for inevitable complications
- Early diagnosis with rapid treatment provides best opportunity for disease-free survival
